name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR Data describes a set of principles for making research data and other digital objects findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable by both people and machines. The principles apply to datasets, software, models, and other research outputs held in repositories and data archives. They do not prescribe a specific technology but set expectations for persistent identifiers, rich metadata, clear access conditions, and standard formats. In practice, FAIR is a spectrum rather than a binary state, and a dataset can be more or less FAIR depending on how well each principle is implemented.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR Data describes a set of principles for making research data and other digital objects findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable by both people and machines. The principles apply to datasets, software, models, and other research outputs held in repositories and data archives. They do not prescribe a specific technology but set expectations for persistent identifiers, rich metadata, clear access conditions, and standard formats. In practice, FAIR is a spectrum rather than a binary state, and a dataset can be more or less FAIR depending on how well each principle is implemented.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data typically runs on institutional or disciplinary data repositories, general-purpose archives, and metadata catalogues that expose structured records through standard interfaces. Persistent identifiers such as DOIs and ORCIDs anchor the findability and citation of data, while metadata schemas like DataCite and Dublin Core provide common descriptive fields. Access protocols such as OAI-PMH and REST APIs allow machines to harvest or query metadata records. Storage may be local, cloud-based, or federated, but the key infrastructure requirement is that identifiers and metadata remain stable and resolvable over time.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Making data FAIR is a curation task that begins with documenting the data's origin, structure, and terms of use in a machine-readable metadata record. Data stewards assign persistent identifiers, choose community-standard vocabularies and ontologies, and describe variables, units, and relationships in a way that other systems can parse. They also select open or standard file formats and provide clear licences and provenance information. Validation against FAIR metrics or checklists helps identify gaps, but the work is iterative and often requires domain expertise to map local data practices to shared standards.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: FAIR data does not mean open data, and access can be restricted or mediated while still being described in a findable and interoperable way. Rights, licences, and conditions for reuse must be stated explicitly in metadata, and provenance records should trace how data was collected, processed, and modified. Repositories and data owners carry responsibility for protecting personal or sensitive information, respecting consent, and managing embargoes. Risk arises when metadata is incomplete, identifiers break, or access conditions are unclear, because downstream users may misinterpret or misuse the data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of FAIR data is toward machine-actionable data that AI systems can discover, assess, and use with minimal human intervention. This includes richer semantic annotations, automated FAIR assessment tools, and tighter links between datasets, models, and code. As AI training and evaluation increasingly depend on curated research data, repositories are likely to adopt more standardised APIs and provenance graphs. The goal is not just compliance with a checklist but data that can reliably support reproducible analysis and trustworthy machine learning workflows.
